claim: Preterm birth leads all causes of death in neonates and children to the age of 5 worldwide.
source: Preterm birth (birth prior to 37 completed weeks of gestation) is a massive global health burden: it leads all causes of death in neonates and children to the age of 5 worldwide (Liu et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2015

claim: Survivors of preterm birth face a broad array of short- and long-term health challenges.
source: survivors face a broad array of short- and long-term health challenges (Blencowe et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Blencowe et al., 2013

claim: Most preterm births in the United States are due to spontaneous onset of preterm labor, with unknown underlying cause.
source: Most preterm births in the United States are due to spontaneous onset of preterm labor, with unknown underlying cause (Goldenberg et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Goldenberg et al., 2008

claim: There currently exist no highly effective interventions that prevent spontaneous preterm birth.
source: there currently exist no highly effective interventions that prevent spontaneous preterm birth (SPTB) (Smith et al., 2009; Romero et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2009 and Romero et al., 2014

claim: The placenta is capable of profoundly influencing both maternal and fetal physiology.
source: The placenta defines the maternal-fetal interface; it is capable of profoundly influencing both maternal and fetal physiology (Kiserud et al., 2006; Shaut et al., 2008; Lykke et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kiserud et al., 2006; Shaut et al., 2008; Lykke et al., 2009

claim: The placenta is subject to remodeling in response to its local environment.
source: it is subject to remodeling in response to its local environment (Genbacev et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Genbacev et al., 1996

claim: Placental disease is known to contribute to preeclampsia.
source: Placental disease is known to contribute to other disorders of pregnancy including preeclampsia (Plaks et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016; Romero and Chaiworapongsa, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Plaks et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016; Romero and Chaiworapongsa, 2013

claim: Placental disease is known to contribute to intrauterine growth restriction.
source: Placental disease is known to contribute to other disorders of pregnancy including preeclampsia (Plaks et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016; Romero and Chaiworapongsa, 2013) and intrauterine growth restriction (McIntyre et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to McIntyre et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021

claim: There is increasing interest in the placenta's potential role as a driver of preterm labor.
source: there is increasing interest in its potential role as a driver of preterm labor (Koga et al., 2009; Pique-Regi et al., 2019; Beharier et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Koga et al., 2009; Pique-Regi et al., 2019; Beharier et al., 2020

claim: Placentas from pregnancies that resulted in spontaneous preterm birth have unique metabolomic and transcriptomic signatures from term counterparts.
source: Recent studies have found that placentas from pregnancies that resulted in SPTB have unique metabolomic and transcriptomic signatures from term counterparts (Elshenawy et al., 2020; Lien et al., 2021; Paquette et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Elshenawy et al., 2020; Lien et al., 2021; Paquette et al., 2018

claim: The reported differences in placentas from spontaneous preterm birth broadly implicate the stress response, inflammation, and various metabolic pathways.
source: The reported differences broadly implicate the stress response, inflammation, and various metabolic pathways.
evidence: Inferred from prior studies on SPTB placentas

claim: Among 326 Gene Expression Omnibus datasets identified by the search terms 'placenta' and 'transcriptome', only 9 included data from normal placenta across a series of gestational timepoints extending to late pregnancy.
source: Upon searching Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) (Edgar et al., 2002) datasets for 'placenta AND transcriptome', we were surprised that among 326 results, only 9 included data from normal placenta across a series of gestational timepoints extending to late pregnancy (Knox and Baker, 2008; Zhou et al., 2009; Loux et al., 2019; Soncin et al., 2018; Maeda et al., 2019; Morey et al., 2021; Steinhauser et al., 2021; Figure 1)
evidence: Supported by data from GEO database search and Figure 1

claim: Weighted gene correlation network analysis of mouse placenta spanning e8.5 to postnatal day 0 revealed distinct gene clusters reflecting groups of genes whose expression changes across timepoints in a unified way.
source: We applied weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA) to a microarray study of mouse placenta (Knox and Baker, 2008) (GEO accession GSE11224) spanning e8.5 to postnatal day 0 (p0) to assess the mRNA signature of the aging mouse placenta, using the dataset with the best temporal resolution across gestation. Distinct clusters emerged, each reflecting a group of genes whose expression changes across timepoints in a unified way (Figure 2A; accompanying statistics available at Mendeley Data, doi: 10.17632/g6vrw9jjn4.1)
evidence: Supported by WGCNA analysis of published microarray data and Figure 2A

claim: Genes in the 'blue' cluster showed increasingly positive correlation with advancing gestational timepoints and include HIF-1 signaling, AMPK signaling, and cellular senescence pathways.
source: Genes in the 'blue' cluster showed increasingly positive correlation with advancing gestational timepoints; KEGG functional pathways significantly overrepresented among these genes include HIF-1 signaling, AMPK signaling, and cellular senescence.
evidence: Supported by WGCNA and KEGG pathway analysis

claim: Genes in the 'turquoise' cluster showed increasingly negative correlation to advancing timepoints and include the citric acid cycle, mitochondrial complex I biogenesis, and the mitotic cell cycle pathways.
source: Genes in the 'turquoise' cluster showed increasingly negative correlation to advancing timepoints; KEGG functional pathways significantly overrepresented among these genes include the citric acid cycle, mitochondrial complex I biogenesis, and the mitotic cell cycle.
evidence: Supported by WGCNA and KEGG pathway analysis

claim: mRNA expression of senescence marker Glb1 peaks at e17.5 in mouse placenta.
source: mRNA expression of senescence marker Glb1 peaks at e17.5 (B; one-way ANOVA p=0.0048)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B with statistical significance

claim: HIF-1 protein abundance is higher at e17.5 versus e13.5 and e15.5 in mouse placenta.
source: HIF-1 protein abundance is higher at e17.5 versus e13.5 and e15.5 (C; one-way ANOVA p=0.019)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C with statistical significance

claim: Expression of HIF-1 targets Hk2 and Slc2a1 increases with advancing gestational age through e17.5 in mouse placenta.
source: as is expression of HIF-1 targets Hk2 and Slc2a1 (D; two-way ANOVA p<0.0001 for gestational age factor)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D with statistical significance

claim: Mitochondrial abundance, reflected by COX IV protein, decreases with gestational age in mouse placenta.
source: Mitochondrial abundance, reflected by COX IV protein, decreases with gestational age (E, one-way ANOVA p=0.0064)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E with statistical significance

claim: Mitochondrial DNA lesion rate peaks at e17.5 in the D-loop region of mouse placenta.
source: mitochondrial DNA lesion rate peaks at e17.5 in the regions of the D-loop (one-way ANOVA p=0.0001)
evidence: Supported by semi-long run qPCR data shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance

claim: Mitochondrial DNA lesion rate peaks at e17.5 in the COII/ATPase6 region of mouse placenta.
source: mitochondrial DNA lesion rate peaks at e17.5 in the regions of the D-loop (one-way ANOVA p=0.0001), COII/ATPase6 (p=0.0027)
evidence: Supported by semi-long run qPCR data shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance

claim: Mitochondrial DNA lesion rate peaks at e17.5 in the ND5 region of mouse placenta.
source: mitochondrial DNA lesion rate peaks at e17.5 in the regions of the D-loop (one-way ANOVA p=0.0001), COII/ATPase6 (p=0.0027), and ND5 (p=0.036)
evidence: Supported by semi-long run qPCR data shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance

claim: There is a modest but significant fetal sex-dependent difference in HIF-1 target expression across gestational timepoints in mouse placenta.
source: Of note, a modest but significant fetal sex-dependent difference in HIF-1 target expression (but not Glb1) was also observed across timepoints (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by subgroup analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Male placentas show consistently higher Slc2a1 expression at all gestational ages compared to female placentas.
source: Subgroup analysis did not reveal sex-dependent mRNA expression changes in Glb1 (A) or Hk2 (B) by qPCR, but did demonstrate consistently higher Slc2a1 expression in male placentas at all gestational ages and an interaction between the effects of sex and gestational age on Slc2a1 expression (C; two-way ANOVA p<0.0001 for sex, p<0.0001 for gestational age, and p=0.028 for interaction)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C with statistical significance

claim: There is an interaction between the effects of sex and gestational age on Slc2a1 expression in mouse placenta.
source: Subgroup analysis did not reveal sex-dependent mRNA expression changes in Glb1 (A) or Hk2 (B) by qPCR, but did demonstrate consistently higher Slc2a1 expression in male placentas at all gestational ages and an interaction between the effects of sex and gestational age on Slc2a1 expression (C; two-way ANOVA p<0.0001 for sex, p<0.0001 for gestational age, and p=0.028 for interaction)
evidence: Supported by two-way ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: mRNA expression of GLB1 and HIF-1 targets HK2 and SLC2A1 trends higher in placentas from >39-week cohort versus <35-week cohort in humans.
source: mRNA expression of senescence marker GLB1 and HIF-1 targets HK2 and SLC2A1 trends higher in placentas from >39-week cohort vs <35-week cohort (A; two-way ANOVA gestational age factor p=0.057)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A with borderline statistical significance

claim: Mitochondrial RNA transcripts ATP6 and COX2 are significantly decreased in human placentas from >39-week cohort versus <35-week cohort.
source: We also examined mitochondrial abundance in the two groups and found that mitochondrial RNA transcripts ATP6 and COX2 were significantly decreased (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B

claim: COX IV protein abundance is lower at the later timepoint (>39 weeks) in human placentas.
source: COX IV protein abundance was lower at the later timepoint (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Maternal age at delivery was significantly different between early (<35 weeks) and late (>39 weeks) gestation groups (31.9±0.9 years versus 36.2±1.0 years, p=0.008).
source: there was a small but statistically significant difference in maternal age at the time of delivery (31.9±0.9 years versus 36.2±1.0 for early gestation versus late, p=0.008)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of maternal characteristics in Table 1

claim: HIF-1 protein accumulates in cultured mouse trophoblasts after 6 hr of CoCl2 exposure.
source: After 6 hr of CoCl2 exposure, we confirmed HIF-1 protein accumulation in cultured trophoblasts (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: After 48 hr of CoCl2 exposure, mouse trophoblasts exhibit decreased mitochondrial abundance by Cox2 mRNA expression.
source: After 48 hr of CoCl2 exposure, mouse trophoblasts exhibit decreased mitochondrial abundance, by Cox2 mRNA expression (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B

claim: After 48 hr of CoCl2 exposure, mouse trophoblasts exhibit decreased Cox IV protein abundance.
source: After 48 hr of CoCl2 exposure, mouse trophoblasts exhibit decreased mitochondrial abundance, by Cox2 mRNA expression (Figure 4B) and Cox IV protein abundance (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C

claim: After 48 hr of CoCl2 exposure, mouse trophoblasts show an increase in senescence marker Glb1.
source: an increase in senescence-associated beta galactosidase (SA-βGal), encoded by Glb1 (Figure 4D)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D

claim: After 48 hr of CoCl2 exposure, mouse trophoblasts show increased senescence-associated beta galactosidase detected by X-gal assay.
source: an increase in senescence-associated beta galactosidase (SA-βGal), encoded by Glb1 (Figure 4D) and detected as a blue stain in an X-gal assay for senescence (Figure 4E)
evidence: Supported by X-gal assay data shown in Figure 4E

claim: HIF-1 is stabilized in CoCl2-treated JAR cells.
source: Consistent with our results in primary cells, we found that HIF-1 is stabilized in CoCl2-treated JAR cells (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A

claim: After 6 days of CoCl2 exposure, mtDNA abundance declined in JAR cells.
source: after 6 days of exposure, mtDNA and protein abundance declined (Figure 5B–C)
evidence: Supported by mtDNA copy number data shown in Figure 5B

claim: After 6 days of CoCl2 exposure, mitochondrial protein abundance declined in JAR cells.
source: after 6 days of exposure, mtDNA and protein abundance declined (Figure 5B–C)
evidence: Supported by COX IV protein data shown in Figure 5C

claim: By 72 hr of CoCl2 exposure, mitochondrial downregulation begins to appear in JAR cells.
source: We further defined the time course of mitochondrial downregulation: by 72 hr the effect began to appear (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by time course data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: At the 6-day timepoint, CoCl2 exposure leads to accumulation of mitochondrial ROS in JAR cells.
source: Furthermore, at the 6-day timepoint we found that CoCl2 exposure leads to accumulation of mitochondrial ROS, as measured by mtSOX, a fluorescent mt-superoxide indicator dye (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by mtSOX fluorescence data shown in Figure 5D

claim: CoCl2 exposure impairs mitochondrial polarization in JAR cells as measured by TMRE staining.
source: impairs mitochondrial polarization, as measured by tetramethylrhodamine ethyl ester (TMRE) staining, a cell-permeant fluorescent dye that accumulates in polarized mitochondria (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 5E

claim: CoCl2-treated JAR cells show morphological hallmarks of cellular senescence including cellular swelling.
source: Additionally, we observed pronounced signs of cellular senescence: morphological hallmarks (cellular swelling) and β-galactosidase overexpression (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5F

claim: CoCl2-treated JAR cells show β-galactosidase overexpression.
source: Additionally, we observed pronounced signs of cellular senescence: morphological hallmarks (cellular swelling) and β-galactosidase overexpression (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by SA-βGal staining data shown in Figure 5F

claim: CoCl2-treated JAR cells exhibit growth arrest which persists for days after removal of the HIF-1 stabilizing compound.
source: growth arrest which persists for days after removal of the HIF-1 stabilizing compound (Figure 5G)
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 5G

claim: CoCl2-treated JAR cells exhibit a senescence-associated secretory phenotype reflected by increases in mRNA expression of VEGF, TNFα, and IL-1α.
source: a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP, Figure 5H) reflected by increases in mRNA expression of the genes encoding VEGF, TNFα, and IL-1α
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5H

claim: CoCl2-treated JAR cells exhibit a senescence-associated secretory phenotype reflected by a decrease in mRNA expression of anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.
source: a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP, Figure 5H) reflected by increases in mRNA expression of the genes encoding VEGF, TNFα, and IL-1α and a decrease in mRNA expression of the gene encoding anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5H

claim: CoCl2 treatment only increased cell death by 0-3% in JAR cells.
source: Propidium iodide staining with quantitative fluorescence cytometry indicated that CoCl2 treatment only increased cell death by 0–3% (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by propidium iodide staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Cells remained adherent and continued to acidify culture medium beyond 14 days of CoCl2 exposure.
source: Importantly, cells remained adherent and continued to acidify culture medium beyond 14 days of CoCl2 exposure
evidence: Observation of cell culture behavior

claim: DMOG, an alternative prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, produces similar effects on HIF-1, mitochondrial abundance and cellular senescence as CoCl2 in JAR cells.
source: Finally, to assess whether the effects we observed were attributable to HIF-1 stabilization and not an off-target effect of CoCl2, we also evaluated an alternative prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, dimethyloxalylglycine (DMOG) (Epstein et al., 2001), and found similar effects on HIF-1, mitochondrial abundance and cellular senescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and citation to Epstein et al., 2001

claim: RNA-Seq revealed upregulation of 2188 genes and downregulation of 1389 genes after CoCl2 treatment in JAR cells.
source: Differential expression (log2 FC>1; false discovery rate [FDR] <0.05) was found for 2188 upregulated and 1389 downregulated genes (Figure 5I)
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5I

claim: Chemical hypoxia led to upregulation of inflammatory signaling in JAR cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis revealed that chemical hypoxia led to upregulation of inflammatory signaling
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-Seq data

claim: Chemical hypoxia led to downregulation of the TCA cycle, mitochondrial biogenesis, and respiratory electron transport in JAR cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis revealed that chemical hypoxia led to upregulation of inflammatory signaling, and downregulation of the TCA cycle, mitochondrial biogenesis, and respiratory electron transport
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-Seq data

claim: Chemical hypoxia in JAR cells recapitulated metabolic patterns that emerged from time course transcriptomic analysis of intact placentas.
source: These data therefore recapitulated metabolic patterns that emerged from time course transcriptomic analysis of intact placentas (Figure 2A)
evidence: Comparison of RNA-Seq results with WGCNA results from Figure 2A

claim: The onset of labor is accompanied by upregulation of contraction-associated proteins including cyclooxygenase-2, prostaglandin F2α receptor, interleukin-6, and connexin 43.
source: The onset of labor is accompanied by a transformation of the uterus from quiescence into a distinct physiologic state in which it generates powerful, coordinated contractions. This phenotypic change is characterized by upregulation of a cadre of contraction-associated proteins (CAPs), notably cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2, encoded by PTGS2), prostaglandin F2α receptor (encoded by PTGFR), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and connexin 43 (Cx43, encoded by GJA1)
evidence: Established knowledge about labor physiology

claim: Phenotypic switching can be modeled in primary and immortalized uterine myocytes upon stimulation with inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β, PGF2α, and thrombin.
source: Phenotypic switching can be modeled in primary and immortalized uterine myocytes upon stimulation with inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β, PGF2α, and thrombin (Nishimura et al., 2020; Rauk and Chiao, 2000; Leimert et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Nishimura et al., 2020; Rauk and Chiao, 2000; Leimert et al., 2019

claim: Co-stimulation of uterine myocytes with IL-1β plus conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 potentiated the induction of PTGS2 mRNA expression.
source: We observed a robust and specific effect: co-stimulation of uterine myocytes with IL-1β plus conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 (but not from untreated JAR cells) potentiated the induction of PTGS2, GJA1, PTGFR, and IL6 mRNA expression (Figure 6A–D)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Co-stimulation of uterine myocytes with IL-1β plus conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 potentiated the induction of GJA1 mRNA expression.
source: We observed a robust and specific effect: co-stimulation of uterine myocytes with IL-1β plus conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 (but not from untreated JAR cells) potentiated the induction of PTGS2, GJA1, PTGFR, and IL6 mRNA expression (Figure 6A–D)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Co-stimulation of uterine myocytes with IL-1β plus conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 potentiated the induction of PTGFR mRNA expression.
source: We observed a robust and specific effect: co-stimulation of uterine myocytes with IL-1β plus conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 (but not from untreated JAR cells) potentiated the induction of PTGS2, GJA1, PTGFR, and IL6 mRNA expression (Figure 6A–D)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Co-stimulation of uterine myocytes with IL-1β plus conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 potentiated the induction of IL6 mRNA expression.
source: We observed a robust and specific effect: co-stimulation of uterine myocytes with IL-1β plus conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 (but not from untreated JAR cells) potentiated the induction of PTGS2, GJA1, PTGFR, and IL6 mRNA expression (Figure 6A–D)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Myocyte contraction is augmented upon exposure to conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 but not from untreated JAR cells.
source: We next employed a collagen lattice assay previously described for assessing contractility of myometrial cells in vitro (Nishimura et al., 2020; Devost and Zingg, 2007), and demonstrated that myocyte contraction is augmented upon exposure to conditioned media from JAR cells treated with CoCl2 but not from untreated JAR cells (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by collagen lattice contraction assay data shown in Figure 6E and citations to Nishimura et al., 2020; Devost and Zingg, 2007

claim: HIF-1 protein is stabilized in placenta following maternal DMOG injection in mice.
source: Analysis of placentas recovered 12 hr following injection indicated that HIF-1 protein is stabilized in placenta following maternal DMOG injection (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Transcription of HIF-1 target genes Hk2 and Slc2a1 was significantly increased following maternal DMOG injection in mice.
source: transcription of HIF-1 target genes Hk2 and Slc2a1 was significantly increased (Figure 7B)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Following injection of DMOG, gestational length was significantly shortened compared to injection of vehicle alone in mice.
source: Following injection of DMOG, gestational length was significantly shortened compared to injection of vehicle alone (Figure 7C–D)
evidence: Supported by gestational length data shown in Figure 7C-D

claim: Advanced gestational timepoints in mouse placenta are accompanied by mitochondrial dysregulation.
source: We report findings stemming from unbiased transcriptomic analysis of mouse placenta, which revealed that hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1) stabilization is a hallmark of advanced gestational timepoints, accompanied by mitochondrial dysregulation

claim: Advanced gestational timepoints in mouse placenta are accompanied by cellular senescence.
source: We report findings stemming from unbiased transcriptomic analysis of mouse placenta, which revealed that hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1) stabilization is a hallmark of advanced gestational timepoints, accompanied by mitochondrial dysregulation and cellular senescence

claim: HIF-1 induction in primary mouse trophoblasts results in cellular senescence.
source: In parallel in primary mouse trophoblasts and human choriocarcinoma cells, we modeled HIF-1 induction and demonstrated resultant mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular senescence

claim: HIF-1 induction in human choriocarcinoma cells results in mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: In parallel in primary mouse trophoblasts and human choriocarcinoma cells, we modeled HIF-1 induction and demonstrated resultant mitochondrial dysfunction

claim: HIF-1 induction in human choriocarcinoma cells results in cellular senescence.
source: In parallel in primary mouse trophoblasts and human choriocarcinoma cells, we modeled HIF-1 induction and demonstrated resultant mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular senescence
evidence: Supported by experimental data in JAR cells

claim: HIF-1 stabilization recapitulated gene signatures observed in aged placenta.

claim: Conditioned media from trophoblasts following HIF-1 induction promoted contractility in immortalized uterine myocytes.
source: Further, conditioned media from trophoblasts following HIF-1 induction promoted contractility in immortalized uterine myocytes

source: Finally, pharmacological induction of HIF-1 via intraperitoneal administration of dimethyloxalyl glycine (DMOG) to pregnant mice caused preterm labor

claim: HIF-1 signaling in late gestation may be a causal determinant of mitochondrial dysfunction observed within the trophoblast.

claim: HIF-1 signaling in late gestation may be a causal determinant of senescence observed within the trophoblast.
source: These results provide clear evidence for placental aging in normal pregnancy, and demonstrate how HIF-1 signaling in late gestation may be a causal determinant of the mitochondrial dysfunction and senescence observed within the trophoblast
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing HIF-1 induction leads to cellular senescence

claim: HIF-1 signaling in late gestation may be a trigger for uterine contraction.
source: These results provide clear evidence for placental aging in normal pregnancy, and demonstrate how HIF-1 signaling in late gestation may be a causal determinant of the mitochondrial dysfunction and senescence observed within the trophoblast as well as a trigger for uterine contraction

claim: The aging placenta may drive the transition from uterine quiescence to contractility at the onset of labor through secreted factors from senescent trophoblasts.

claim: Cobalt chloride is a prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor that stabilizes HIF-1α.

claim: Two mouse models with constitutively active placental HIF-1 induced from the beginning of gestation showed impaired spiral artery remodeling.
source: Two important recent studies have examined separate mouse models with constitutively active placental HIF-1 and found that when induced from the beginning of gestation, placental HIF-1 signaling drives abnormal placentogenesis and impaired spiral artery remodeling, leading to placental hypoperfusion, fetal growth restriction, and a preeclampsia-like clinical syndrome (Albers et al., 2019; Sallais et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Albers et al., 2019; Sallais et al., 2022

claim: Two mouse models with constitutively active placental HIF-1 induced from the beginning of gestation showed placental hypoperfusion.
